reasoning: Preserved all four failure-driven edits, including narrated-task tracking, endpoint coverage and cardinality checks, schema auditing, and required call ordering. Omitted the success-driven cardinality edit because its core guidance is already covered by the higher-priority failure edit, which requires matching requested result counts to endpoint support and quantity fields. No edits target the protected section.

edits.target: - Turn each explicit clause into a requested action, target, and set of qualifiers. In one-turn tasks, narrated sequences such as “first,” “then,” and “finally” describe requested actions, not actions already completed.
edits.content: - Turn each explicit clause into a requested action, target, and set of qualifiers. In one-turn tasks, treat imperative sequences and narrative or retrospective sequences (for example, “the user first accessed ... then retrieved ...”) as requested actions unless the prompt explicitly says they were completed outside this task. Before choosing tools, make an internal ledger in query order with one row per requested operation and result; expand listed targets and sources, including those in later or final clauses. Match every row to a call and every call to a row, without treating related searches as coverage of distinct results. Group rows into one call only when the endpoint explicitly supports doing so.

edits.target: - Choose an endpoint by its documented operation, output, target, and support for the requested qualifiers—not merely by a shared topic or entity name. Prefer the most specific endpoint that fits the request; use separate endpoints when distinct deliverables require them.
edits.content: - When endpoints overlap, classify the requested result and operation, then compare them with the specific endpoint’s documented output and fields—not provider-level marketing text or a shared topic or entity name. A deliverable is covered only if that endpoint returns the requested result with its qualifiers (for example, people versus events, verification versus a related risk check, or a named-source feed versus a general topic search). Match cardinality as well: use an endpoint that supports the requested number of results and provide its quantity field when available. Every emitted call must map to an explicit requested outcome.

edits.target: - Carry every explicit filter and qualifier into the supported field that represents it. Follow the endpoint’s documented parameter meanings, required and optional fields, value types, canonical values, units, and encoding for multiple values. Do not assume conventions are the same across providers.
edits.content: - Bind each qualifier only to the operation it modifies, and include it only on endpoints whose schemas support it. For hierarchical filters, map each level to its documented field and honor stated dependencies rather than substituting one level for another. Before serialization, audit each call against its schema: include every required parameter as a correctly formed name/value pair, put optional parameters in the designated optional slot when the contract provides one, avoid bare names or placeholders, and preserve declared value types and exact enum or canonical values.

edits.target: - Follow the active prompt’s answer contract. Represent each invocation as its own call object with exactly the required keys and value types; keep calls in the required wrapper and do not merge calls or duplicate fields.
edits.content: - Follow the active prompt’s answer contract. Represent each invocation as its own call object with exactly the required keys and value types; keep calls in the required wrapper and do not merge calls or duplicate fields. If the contract specifies an order (for example, sorting by tool name), reorder complete call objects to match it; do not let query or clause order override the required order.
